meta.title: Clinically-Inspired Hierarchical Multi-Label Classification of Chest X-rays with a Penalty-Based Loss Function
meta.venue: arXiv:2502.03591v1, submitted to IEEE (IEEE Transactions format)
meta.institution: Concordia University (Gina Cody School, Montreal); YULCOM Technologies (Montreal); McGill University Health Centre
meta.code_repo: CIHMLC (public Git repository, linked in paper)

meta.relevance_to_our_paper: Nearest prior work. We adopt the HBCE penalty concept but with critical differences: (1) their penalty is a HARD INDICATOR, ours uses ReLU (differentiable); (2) they train from scratch on CheXpert only, we use TorchXRayVision pretrained weights on 6 pooled datasets; (3) they have no inference-time fallback gate — we add MC-Dropout variance gating.

critical_corrections_vs_prior_json: Institution is Concordia University + YULCOM + McGill — NOT unknown
Dataset is CheXpert ONLY with VisualCheXbert-derived labels — NOT pooled multi-dataset
Architecture trained FROM SCRATCH (random init) — NOT TorchXRayVision pretrained
Dropout rate is p=0.5 — NOT p=0.2
Penalty formula is a HARD INDICATOR FUNCTION — NOT a ReLU product
Data-driven penalty = empirical co-occurrence ratio with Laplace smoothing — distinct from any formula in our draft
MC-Dropout passes N=10 — NOT T=30 (our project uses T=30)
AUROC 0.892 on 5 CheXpert labels (our comparable metric), NOT 0.903 (that is over all hierarchy labels)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.purpose: Clinical need → gap in prior hierarchical models → proposed solution

verbatim_key_claims: Multi-label classification for diagnosing wide range from CXR is important
Complex and overlapping thoracic diseases: capturing label dependencies improves diagnostic reliability
Lung pathologies: leading cause of morbidity/mortality globally [1]
Diagnostic variability due to experience/expertise differences
Long working hours impair concentration, increase diagnostic errors [2]
Global shortage of radiologists, especially in low-resource settings [3]
Many DL approaches struggle to incorporate clinical hierarchies effectively
Hierarchical classification models do not sufficiently leverage clinical insights through penalties or parent-child relationships
This limits both interpretability and performance
Hierarchical multi-label classification framework organizing labels into parent-child relationships
Novel HBCE loss: applies penalties when child predicted positive without corresponding parent positive
Two penalty strategies: fixed penalty (constant β) and data-driven penalty (empirical co-occurrence ratio)
Primary objective: improve clinical interpretability via hierarchical groupings that mirror clinical decision-making
In clinical practice: most dangerous/life-threatening diagnoses ruled out first, then less severe
CXR reviewed by NON-radiology trained professionals in inpatient settings — interpretability critical
Custom hierarchical loss improves model performance and explainability
subsections.writing_note: This paragraph explicitly states the clinical workflow motivation for a hierarchy — rule out dangerous before workup for mild. Use same framing in our intro: 'model should preferentially commit to a broad safe prediction when uncertain, rather than asserting a specific wrong diagnosis.'

verbatim_key_claims: Weighted AUROC 0.9034 on CheXpert test set, single-model single-run
Data-driven penalties show potential to improve predictive accuracy
Visual explanations and uncertainty estimations enhance interpretability and transparency
All code, model configurations, experiment details publicly available

sections.title: Related Work
sections.purpose: Survey multi-label CXR methods and hierarchical learning methods; each subsection ends leading toward the gap

subsections.title: Multi-Label Classification in Medical Imaging

key_papers_cited.name: CheXtransfer
key_papers_cited.method: Benchmark of 16 CNN architectures on CheXpert

key_papers_cited.name: Transfer learning study
key_papers_cited.method: Fine-tuning, layer transfer, combined transfer on CXR

subsections.summary_sentence: Recent methods shift toward hybrid architectures, semantic embedding, and curriculum learning — but all treat label dependencies as co-occurrence or learned structure, NOT as clinical IS-A relationships with enforced penalty.
subsections.writing_note: Asadi surveys 6+ non-hierarchical papers. All of them achieve higher than 0.800 on CheXpert. The survey shows familiarity with the field, not just the hierarchical subset. Include non-hierarchical baselines in our Related Work too.

subsections.title: Hierarchical Learning in Medical Imaging

key_papers_cited.name: HMCN
key_papers_cited.method: Hierarchical multi-label classification networks — first explicit hierarchy in DNN for multi-label

key_papers_cited.name: HMLC
key_papers_cited.method: Two-stage: conditional probs within hierarchy (sibling), then finetuned unconditional; PLCO+PadChest; AUROC 0.887 on PLCO

key_papers_cited.name: CT+LSR
key_papers_cited.method: Conditional training (parent-positive subset) + label smoothing; CheXpert; AUROC 0.884 single model, 0.940 ensemble

subsections.gap_statement: HMCNs and related approaches incorporate hierarchy at TRAINING TIME (data selection, conditional objectives). This study opts for a SINGLE-RUN training pipeline with a PENALTY-BASED LOSS that enforces consistency without multi-stage training.
subsections.writing_note: Table III (at the end of the paper) shows the comparison table. Pham et al. [19] is the strongest baseline: 0.884 single model. Our paper (0.892) is only marginally better — the value is in the clinical interpretability and single-run simplicity.

sections.title: Methodology
sections.purpose: Full reproducible description; 7 subsections covering novelty, dataset, hierarchy, architecture, loss, training, UQ, visualization

subsections.title: Novelty and Divergence from Prior Work
verbatim_key_claims: Emphasizes clinical interpretability and explainability while maintaining strong performance
Penalty-based loss enforces consistency between child and parent labels — addresses clinically implausible predictions
Not commonly seen in traditional dependency models (co-occurrence, GCN)
Hierarchical models use multi-stage training; this study opts for SINGLE-RUN pipeline
Simplifies process, reduces computational complexity (but may limit nuanced hierarchical learning)
subsections.writing_note: This is a rare explicit 'Novelty' subsection. It pre-empts reviewer confusion. Use when: (a) nearest prior work appears to solve the same problem, (b) the difference is subtle (single-run vs. multi-stage is easy to miss). Our paper should consider this.

subsections.title: Dataset and Labeling Strategy
verbatim_key_claims: CheXpert dataset: 224K+ CXRs from 65K+ patients
Labels: VisualCheXbert-derived (NOT standard CheXpert or CheXbert labelers — different tool)
Splits: Train=223,414 / Validation=234 / Test=668
Directly using CheXpert labels poses limitations due to interdependence of pathologies
Introduced new parent categories based on clinical insights (e.g., 'Fluid Accumulation' for Pleural Effusion + Pneumonia + Edema + Consolidation)
Added 'Uncertain' label: instances with neither positive findings nor 'No Finding' → captures clinical uncertainty

subsections.title: Clinical Relevance of the Groupings
rationale_bullets: Grouping Related Conditions: enlarged cardiac silhouette → primary cardiac dx; gravity-dependent opacifications → fluid infiltration spectrum
Parent-Child Dependencies: consolidations could precede pneumonia — hierarchy captures this clinically
Improved Interpretability: broad dx first (lung opacity vs. cardiac), then specific child (Cardiomegaly under Cardiac) — mirrors clinical workflow
Capturing Clinical Uncertainty: Uncertain category → model can acknowledge ambiguous cases, may indicate CT needed
informed_by: clinical feedback from co-author Ian J. Gerard (McGill radiation oncology)

subsections.writing_note: Their hierarchy has a ROOT node ('Abnormal') with intermediate parent nodes (e.g., 'Fluid Accumulation') that are NOT in the original CheXpert labels — these are INVENTED PARENT LABELS. Our project uses Indonesian clinical guidelines (PDPI/PNPK/KKI) as authority for IS-A edges, which is different.

subsections.title: Model Architecture
verbatim_key_claims: DenseNet121 [7] as base: widespread in medical imaging, dense connectivity, vanishing gradient mitigation, feature reuse
Model initialized with RANDOM WEIGHTS and trained FROM SCRATCH (NOT ImageNet or CXR pretrained)
Rationale for scratch: 'domain-specific nature of CXR images often benefits from task-specific training [23]'
Image size: 320×320 (higher resolution than standard 224×224)
architecture_layers: Conv2D: 512 filters (after backbone, to enhance fine feature extraction for hierarchy)
Global Average Pooling (reduces overfitting vs. FC layer, maintains spatial features)
Dense: 128 neurons + ReLU (nonlinearity, complex feature interactions)
Dropout: p=0.5 (prevent overfitting; also reused at inference for MC-Dropout)
Dense: N_labels neurons + sigmoid (multi-label output probabilities)
subsections.writing_note: CRITICAL DIFFERENCE FROM OUR PAPER: Asadi trains from scratch. We use TorchXRayVision pretrained weights (densenet121-res224-all). This is a major architectural choice to highlight in our Related Work or Methods. Also: their dropout is p=0.5, ours is p=0.2 — affects MC-Dropout uncertainty calibration.

subsections.title: Clinically-Inspired Hierarchical Loss Function
subsections.purpose: Define BCE base → add indicator-based penalty → explain fixed vs. data-driven modes

subsections.title: Binary Cross-Entropy (base)
subsections.equation: L_BCE(ytrue, ypred) = -(1/B) Σ_b Σ_l [y_true^(b,l) log(y_pred^(b,l)) + (1-y_true^(b,l)) log(1-y_pred^(b,l))]   [Eq.1]
subsections.note: Standard BCE over all labels, no masking mentioned explicitly for not-applicable labels

subsections.title: Hierarchical Penalty (hard indicator)
subsections.meaning: Penalty fires when child is predicted confident-positive (>0.5) but parent is predicted confident-negative (<0.5). HARD THRESHOLD — not differentiable at 0.5.
subsections.critical_difference_from_our_paper: Our methods draft uses ReLU(p_c - 0.5) * ReLU(0.5 - p_g) — this is the DIFFERENTIABLE APPROXIMATION of Asadi's indicator. Both penalize the same inconsistency but ours provides gradient information everywhere.

fixed.note: Constant for all parent-child pairs; β=1 used in experiments
fixed.properties: Computationally simple; not adaptive to actual label co-occurrence rates

data_driven.meaning: Empirical probability that child=1 given parent=0 in training set; Laplace-smoothed with ε
data_driven.correlation_range: Asadi found parent-child correlation ranges from 0.814 to 0.999
data_driven.winner: Data-driven at λ=0.5 achieves highest AUROC — selected as final method

total_loss.note: λ controls penalty strength relative to BCE; swept over 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0 in experiments

subsections.title: Training Strategy

verbatim_details.lr_schedule: ReduceLROnPlateau: factor 0.9 when validation loss plateaus
verbatim_details.early_stopping: Patience=3 consecutive epochs without val loss decrease
verbatim_details.checkpointing: Save when either val loss decreased OR AUROC increased
verbatim_details.augmentation_note: Seed fixed for batch reproducibility but augmentations allowed to vary
verbatim_details.no_horizontal_flip_note: THEY DO USE horizontal flip (unlike our project which disables it for situs inversus reason)

subsections.writing_note: Our project disables horizontal flip because it mirrors cardiac silhouette (situs inversus issue). Asadi does NOT make this distinction — they flip horizontally. This is a methodological difference worth noting.

subsections.title: Monte Carlo Uncertainty Estimation
verbatim_key_claims: MC-Dropout during inference: multiple forward passes with active dropout
Yields distribution of predictions
Compute mean and standard deviation for each label
Mean = predictive confidence; Std = uncertainty measure
N=10 Monte Carlo iterations (confirmed in Fig 3 caption)
Provides clinicians information on reliability of model results
subsections.critical_difference_from_our_paper: Asadi uses N=10 passes; our project uses T=30. More passes = better approximation but slower inference. Also: Asadi's dropout p=0.5 means more variance per pass; ours p=0.2 means less noise.

subsections.title: Class Activation Maps
verbatim_key_claims: Grad-CAM [8] on final convolutional layer
Heatmaps indicate regions most strongly influencing predictions
Backpropagate gradients of target class through final conv layer
Activations normalized and clipped at 0.5 threshold (retain most prominent regions only)
Discretized colormap: enhances contrast between high (black=1) and low (white=0) activation
Allows clinicians to verify model attention aligns with auscultation findings (lungs, heart)

sections.title: Results
sections.purpose: Uncertain label ablation → penalty ablation (fixed vs. data-driven, scale factors) → overall performance → visualization

subsections.title: Uncertain Label
verbatim_key_claims: Compared 14-label (without Uncertain) vs 15-label (with Uncertain) models
Mean AUROC: 0.890 (without) vs 0.892 (with) on all 14 pathology labels
Paired t-test: NOT significant (5-label p=0.0976; 14-label p=0.2076)
Conclusion: Uncertain label marginally better AUROC, may hold CLINICAL importance for ambiguous cases
Flat training WITH Uncertain achieves highest 5-label mean: 0.899
subsections.note: Interesting: the flat model WITH Uncertain (0.899) actually outperforms the hierarchical models (0.892) on the 5 standard CheXpert labels. Hierarchy hurts slightly on the standard benchmark but improves interpretability.

subsections.title: Penalty
verbatim_key_claims: Experiments: 1 hierarchy × 2 penalty types × 4 scale factors (0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0)
Parent-child correlations range 0.814 to 0.999 → used fixed β=1 for fair comparison
Data-driven significantly better for Missing Lung Tissue, Opacity (high-level; p=0.0351, 0.0003)
Data-driven significantly better for Atelectasis, Edema, Lung Opacity (low-level; p=0.0038, 0.0225, 0.0001)
Data-driven λ=0.5: highest mean AUROC 0.903, best Abnormal (0.942), Fluid Accumulation (0.922), Other (0.903)
subsections.table_I_summary: 5-label comparison: flat+Uncertain (0.899) > data-driven 0.5 (0.892) > fixed 0.3 (0.888). Hierarchical models DO NOT beat flat on standard 5-label benchmark.
subsections.table_II_summary: High-level categories: data-driven 0.5 wins overall (0.904 mean). Fixed 0.3 wins on Cardiac (0.862) and Other (0.900).

subsections.title: Overall Model Performance
verbatim_key_claims: Mean AUROC 0.903 on all hierarchy labels
Mean AUROC 0.904 on high-level categories (Table II)
Mean AUROC 0.892 on 5 standard CheXpert labels (Table III)
Table III comparison: marginally better than Zhang et al. [10] (p=0.0598); no significant difference between all methods
subsections.honest_assessment: Asadi's hierarchical model (0.892) only marginally outperforms flat Irvin baseline (0.889) and Liu MLLGL (0.889) on the 5-label benchmark. The contribution is primarily in interpretability and single-run simplicity, not raw AUROC.

subsections.title: Visualization
verbatim_key_claims: Grad-CAMs shown for one sample image with activations for all hierarchy labels
Activations clipped at 0.5 threshold; segmented colormap for clarity
Fluid Accumulation: high activation over potential fluid-affected areas (consistent with Pleural Effusion, Edema)
Cardiomegaly, Lung Opacity, Enlarged Cardiomediastinum: targeted focus in heart region
MC-Dropout uncertainty shown per label: prediction ± std (N=10)

figure_3_details.rows: Top: high-level + Uncertain; Middle: original CheXpert labels; Bottom: child labels
figure_3_details.ground_truth: Atelectasis, Cardiomegaly, Edema, Enlarged Cardiomegaly, Lung Opacity, Pleural Effusion

sections.title: Discussion
verbatim_key_claims: Hierarchical structure: key strength for interpretability (aligns label dependencies with medical expertise)
Custom HBCE loss: ensures logical consistency between predictions
Single-run pipeline: simplifies deployment, reduces computational overhead
CAMs + MC-Dropout: transparency for clinicians
Comparison to prior work (Table III): highest AUROC for Atelectasis (0.879) and Pleural Effusion (0.945); mean AUROC 0.892 similar to SOTA
Marginally better than Zhang et al. [10] (p=0.0598); NO significant difference between all methods
limitations_stated: Batch size affects model: smaller batches improve generalization but noisier gradients
Model's reliance on specific label structure reduces generalizability across datasets
sections.writing_note: Asadi is honest: 'no significant difference found between all these methods.' The claim is clinical value, not SOTA AUROC. Our paper should position similarly: AUROC competitiveness + novel inference-time mechanism + uncertainty characterization as contribution.

sections.title: Conclusion
verbatim_key_claims: Enhanced interpretability and clinical relevance via hierarchical label structure + custom loss
Organized pathologies into clinically meaningful categories reflecting clinical decision-making
HBCE loss: flexible fixed and data-driven penalty schemes; data-driven improves AUROC
Weighted AUROC 0.9034 on CheXpert (full hierarchy); single-model, single-run
CAM + MC-Dropout: model decision-making transparency and confidence measures
Bridges gap between automated classification and clinical application
future_work: Adaptive batch size strategies (combine small-batch generalization + large-batch stability)
Domain adaptation approach: dynamically align hierarchy to target dataset

structural_lessons: Explicit §III.A 'Novelty and Divergence' subsection is effective when gap vs. prior is subtle. State the distinction in one sentence: 'multi-stage training (prior) vs. single-run penalty-loss (ours).'
§II.A surveys ~6 non-hierarchical papers before §II.B surveys hierarchical. Pattern: show breadth, then depth. Cite performance numbers (AUROC) for every surveyed paper.
Results section ablates in dependency order: Uncertain label first (baseline setup), then Penalty (core contribution). Each ablation references specific Tables.
Discussion is honest about statistical significance: 'no significant difference between methods.' Frame contribution as interpretability, not raw accuracy.
Table III comparison: only 2 methods marked * (hierarchical) — Pham et al. and Ours. Signals that hierarchical is the relevant comparison class.
Figure 3 shows CAM for ALL labels simultaneously on one image — qualitative evidence of per-label spatial attention. This is a common and effective visualization for multi-label CXR papers.

penalty_formula.asadi: Hard indicator: P_{p,c} = β · 1{p_child > 0.5 AND p_parent < 0.5}  (non-differentiable at threshold)
penalty_formula.ours: Smooth ReLU product: penalty(g,c) = ReLU(p_c - 0.5) * ReLU(0.5 - p_g)  (differentiable everywhere)
penalty_formula.implication: Our formulation provides gradient signal even for predictions close to 0.5; Asadi's formula gives zero gradient in the transition zone

backbone.ours: DenseNet121 from TorchXRayVision pretrained weights (densenet121-res224-all, trained on 6 CXR datasets)

label_authority.asadi: Custom clinician-defined hierarchy (parent nodes invented for the paper, validated by clinician co-author)
label_authority.ours: Indonesian PDPI/PNPK/KKI clinical guidelines (external authority, 51 canonical labels)

inference_mechanism.asadi: No inference-time fallback. Predictions are raw sigmoid outputs. Uncertainty only shown qualitatively via Grad-CAM + MC-Dropout std.
inference_mechanism.ours: Inference-time gate: if sigma_c > tau_u (uncertain), suppress child prediction, fall back to parent or abstain.

differentiation_from_our_paper.suggested_cite_sentence: Asadi et al. (2025) propose a hierarchical BCE loss with a penalty term that fires when a child label is predicted positive while its parent is negative. Unlike their hard-threshold indicator, our formulation uses a differentiable ReLU approximation to enable gradient-based optimization throughout. Moreover, while Asadi et al. apply hierarchical structure only at training time, we extend the hierarchy to inference by using MC-Dropout variance as a gate that falls back to a coarser parent prediction when per-label uncertainty exceeds a threshold.
